# Diagnostic procedures in gynecology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Basics of obstetrics and gynecology > Diagnostic procedures in gynecology*

[Original Article Link](/library/SN0y0g)

---

## Summary

A complete <u>gynecological examination</u> includes inspection of the <u>vagina</u> with the aid of a speculum and, if needed, <u>colposcopy</u> and bimanual palpation. <u>Speculum examination</u> is also used to facilitate obtaining smears for cytological and microbiological studies. Depending on the clinical presentation, other laboratory diagnostics and imaging procedures may be indicated. <u>MRI</u> scans and/or ultrasounds of the <u>breast</u>, for example, may supplement standard <u>screening tests</u> such as <u>mammography</u>. Unexplained <u>pelvic</u> symptoms may require <u>transvaginal ultrasonography</u> or more invasive diagnostic procedures such as <u>endometrial sampling</u> and hysteroscopic or <u>laparoscopic</u> examination.

---

## Speculum examination

* Insertion of a speculum device facilitates the inspection of the vaginal wall and <u>ectocervix</u>

* Evaluate the quality of vaginal discharge to determine whether a smear should be acquired

* The amount of <u>vaginal discharge</u> varies by individual and by the stage of <u>the menstrual cycle</u>

* Signs that <u>vaginal discharge</u> may be pathologic

* Malodorous (e.g., fishy)

* Abnormal consistency (e.g., frothy, curd-like)

* Bloody, brown, yellow, green, or gray color

* Symptoms indicating pathologic discharge

* Pruritic and/or <u>erythematous</u> <u>vagina</u>

* Cervical tenderness

* See <u>differential diagnoses of infectious causes of vaginal discharge</u>

* Physiologic leukorrhea

* Profuse white or yellow and non-malodorous <u>vaginal discharge</u> can be physiological if none of the features mentioned above are present.

* In <u>newborns</u>, <u>vaginal discharge</u> may occur due to in-utero exposure to maternal <u>estrogen</u> (no treatment is necessary).





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Speculum examination</u> is virtually never indicated in preadolescent patients! If absolutely necessary (e.g., <u>vaginal bleeding</u>, trauma, abuse), it is usually performed under <u>general anesthesia</u>!

## Genital swabs

### Vaginal swab




#### Types [[4]](/library/-71DoR0)[[5]](/library/0H1eKR0)




* High vaginal swab (HVS)

* Taken from the <u>posterior</u> <u>vaginal fornix</u>, where cervical and vaginal secretions pool in the <u>supine position</u>

* Obtained by a <u>health care provider</u> during <u>per speculum examination</u>

* Low vaginal swab (LVS)

* Taken from the mid to <u>distal</u> end of the <u>vagina</u>

* Obtained by patients themselves or by a <u>health care provider</u> when <u>per speculum examination</u> is not required  [[6]](/library/KBcUbU0)[[7]](/library/ZH1ZKR0)





#### Tests




* Vaginal pH

* Normal <u>vaginal pH</u>: 4–4.5

* <u>pH</u> > 4.5 → suspect <u>bacterial vaginosis</u> and <u>trichomoniasis</u> (other causes of increased <u>vaginal pH</u> include <u>menstruation</u>, <u>amniotic fluid</u>, and sexual intercourse)

* Vaginal wet mount preparation

* Definition: a sample of <u>vaginal discharge</u> is transferred to a slide and mixed with <u>normal saline</u> or <u>potassium</u> hydroxide (KOH) before examining under a microscope.

* Normal findings: cylindrical Lactobacilli (Doderlein's bacilli)

* Pathological findings:





| <br>Finding<br> | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| Motile flagellated <u>protozoa</u> | <u>Trichomoniasis</u> |
| <br><u>Pseudomycelia</u> and/or <u>yeast</u> cells on a <u>KOH preparation</u><br> | <u>Vaginal candidiasis</u> |
| <br><u>Clue cells</u> and a positive <u>whiff test</u> (adding KOH to <u>vaginal smear</u> elicits a fishy odor) | <u>Bacterial vaginosis</u> |





* <u>Gram staining</u> can reveal gram-negative, intracellular <u>diplococci</u> in patients with <u>gonorrhea</u>.  [[8]](/library/aH1QKR0)

* Perform a <u>nucleic acid amplification test</u> if <u>chlamydia</u>, <u>gonorrhea</u>, <u>trichomoniasis</u>, or <u>genital herpes</u> is suspected.





### Endocervical swab




* A swab of mucus and cells from the <u>endocervix</u> taken by a <u>health care provider</u> during <u>per speculum examination</u>

* Obtained in order to perform a <u>nucleic acid amplification test</u> if <u>cervicitis</u> or <u>pelvic inflammatory disease</u> is suspected

* For <u>cervical cytology</u> in the screening of <u>cervical cancer</u>, see <u>Papanicolaou test</u>.

---

## Colposcopy

* Colposcope: a type of microscope used to acquire a magnified view of the <u>ectocervix</u> or vaginal wall

* <u>Colposcopy</u>: A diagnostic procedure to evaluate the <u>cervix</u>, <u>vagina</u>, and <u>vulva</u> using a <u>colposcope</u>; allows for assessment of the <u>ectocervix</u> under magnification (6–40 x)

* Application of <u>acetic acid</u> or <u>iodine</u> facilitates the colposcopic detection of precancerous and cancerous lesions

* <u>Colposcopy</u>-directed <u>cervical smears</u> and <u>biopsies</u>

* Surgical procedures under colposcopic guidance





### Benign lesions




* No further evaluation necessary

* Cervical ectopy: a state in which the <u>squamous cell epithelium</u> of the <u>ectocervix</u> is replaced by columnar cell <u>epithelium</u> of the <u>endocervix</u> under the physiological influence of <u>estrogen</u> (e.g., <u>pregnancy</u>, certain <u>oral contraceptives</u>). <u>Cervical ectopy</u> is seen on <u>colposcopy</u> as a sharply demarcated bright red area with <u>papillary</u> structures.

* Clinical features: mostly asymptomatic; occasional <u>postcoital bleeding</u> and <u>vaginal discharge</u>

* Predisposition to <u>chlamydial infection</u>

* Malignant transformation may occur in cases of <u>HPV</u>-16 and/or <u>HPV</u>-18 infections.

* Transformation zone: the area between the non-keratinized <u>squamous epithelium</u> of the <u>ectocervix</u> and the <u>columnar epithelium</u> of the <u>endocervix</u>. The transformation zone is a common site for infections and <u>dysplastic</u> changes.

* Nabothian cysts: retention cysts that arise in the transformation zone . These cysts have no pathological significance.

* Cervical polyps: <u>hyperplastic</u> cervical <u>epithelium</u>

* Clinical features: <u>vaginal bleeding</u>

* Malignant degeneration is rare

* Treatment: surgical resection of the polyp and cauterization of the polyp's pedicle to prevent recurrence





### Abnormal findings




* Require further evaluation

* White lesions under <u>acetic acid</u> application: <u>condylomata acuminata</u>

* White membrane that cannot be scraped off: <u>cervical leukoplakia</u>

* Punctate lesions or coarse <u>mosaic</u> pattern: <u>cervical intraepithelial neoplasia</u>

* Atypical vessels: <u>cervical cancer</u>





References:[[9]](/library/3EaSvm)[[10]](/library/LfYw5o)[[11]](/library/ofY0Mo)[[12]](/library/KfYUMo)

## Laboratory tests

Depending on the clinical presentation, other laboratory tests may be indicated:




* <u>Inflammatory parameters</u> if adnexitis, <u>mastitis</u>, and/or <u>endometritis</u> are suspected

* <u>Pregnancy test</u>

* <u>Hormone</u> levels for work-up of <u>infertility</u>

* <u>Renal function tests</u> and <u>urinalysis</u> if urinary symptoms are present

* Serum <u>transaminase</u> (<u>AST</u>, <u>ALT</u>) and <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> (<u>ALP</u>) levels, If <u>liver</u> or <u>bone metastases</u> are suspected

* <u>Tumor markers</u>

* <u>CA 15-3</u>: <u>breast carcinoma</u>

* <u>CA 125</u>: ovarian and/or <u>endometrial carcinoma</u>

* <u>SCC</u>: <u>squamous cell carcinomas</u> (e.g., cervical, vulval, and/or <u>vaginal carcinomas</u>)

* <u>AFP</u>: <u>germ cell tumors</u>

* <u>HCG</u>: <u>choriocarcinomas</u> and/or <u>germ cell tumors</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Always perform a <u>pregnancy test</u> if a woman of child-bearing age presents with lower abdominal <u>pain</u>!References:[[13]](/library/qfYCMo)[[14]](/library/IfYYno)

## Ultrasound

### Transabdominal <u>ultrasound</u>




* An abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> is the easiest method of assessing the <u>uterus</u>, <u>ovaries</u>, and adnexal structures.

* Assessment of:

* Urogenital tract

* Assessment of <u>fetal development</u> (see <u>ultrasonography</u> during <u>pregnancy</u>)

* <u>Pelvic</u> organs





### Transvaginal ultrasound




* <u>Ovaries</u>: Performed to diagnose <u>ovarian cysts</u>, tumors, and follicular maturation

* <u>Uterus</u>

* <u>Myometrium</u> (e.g., to diagnose <u>leiomyomas</u>)

* <u>Endometrium</u>

* Echogenic layer in the long axis view of the <u>uterus</u> (referred to as the “endometrial stripe”)

* <u>Endometrial</u> thickness varies with <u>the menstrual cycle</u>

* <u>Postmenopausal</u> women with an <u>endometrial</u> thickness greater than 8 mm should undergo a follow-up <u>ultrasound</u> after 1–3 months

* <u>Postmenopausal</u> women with an <u>endometrial</u> thickness greater than 10 mm should undergo <u>hysteroscopy</u> and <u>endometrial</u> <u>curettage</u> to rule out <u>endometrial carcinoma</u>.

* Assessment of <u>fetal development</u> during the <u>first trimester</u>

* Measurement of cervical length in cases of <u>cervical incompetence</u>

### Breast ultrasound




<u>Breast ultrasound</u> can be used to assess <u>breast</u> lesions which were detected by palpation, <u>mammography</u>, and/or <u>breast</u> <u>MRI</u> scans. <u>Ultrasound</u> can also be used to assess the <u>axilla</u> for <u>lymph node</u> involvement if there is suspicion for <u>breast cancer</u>.
